content:
**Quick answer:** Arthritis in the knees can cause pain, stiffness, swelling and difficulty walking, climbing stairs or getting up from a chair. Treatment depends on the type and severity of arthritis and may include exercise, physiotherapy, weight management where appropriate, pain management and medical treatment. Gentle movement, pacing and practical adaptations can support day-to-day function.

## What it feels like

Knee arthritis can cause pain or aching, stiffness, swelling, tenderness, reduced movement, difficulty fully bending or straightening the knee, discomfort after sitting, and difficulty walking, using stairs or getting up from a chair. Symptoms often vary from day to day.

Early signs can be subtle: recurring knee discomfort, stiffness after sitting, discomfort during or after activity, difficulty with stairs, reduced confidence bending the knee, occasional swelling, or changes in how easily you walk. Symptoms do not always progress predictably, and mild knee pain does not automatically mean severe arthritis will develop.

Pain alone cannot tell you exactly what is happening inside a joint. If symptoms are persistent, worsening or unexplained, seek medical advice rather than diagnosing yourself.

## What causes it

Osteoarthritis is particularly common in the knees. It involves changes to cartilage, bone and other tissues within and around the joint, and it should not simply be described as the knee being "worn out".

Rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune inflammatory condition, can also affect the knees, sometimes both. Other forms of arthritis and joint disease can affect a knee too: gout, for example, can cause sudden, severe joint inflammation. A painful or swollen knee should not automatically be assumed to be osteoarthritis.

## How it is diagnosed

Diagnosis starts with your symptoms and a clinical assessment. A healthcare professional may ask where your knee hurts, how long symptoms have been present, whether it swells, when stiffness is worst, which activities are difficult, whether other joints are affected and whether you have other symptoms, then examine how the knee moves and assess swelling, tenderness and function.

Tests or imaging may sometimes be appropriate, but not everyone with suspected osteoarthritis needs an X-ray before treatment or self-management can begin.

## Treatment options

Treatment depends on the type of arthritis. For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends a core approach that includes therapeutic exercise and information and support, with weight management for people who are overweight or living with obesity where appropriate. Wider options include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, pain management, medicines recommended or prescribed by an appropriate healthcare professional, injections in selected circumstances, and surgery for some people with severe symptoms.

On injections, NICE says intra-articular corticosteroid injections can be considered for osteoarthritis in selected situations, with any benefit generally short term. Knee replacement may be considered when osteoarthritis has a substantial effect on quality of life and non-surgical management is no longer providing enough benefit, but having knee arthritis does not automatically mean you will need one.

On braces and supports: NICE does not recommend routinely offering devices such as braces, supports, insoles or walking aids to everyone with osteoarthritis unless there is a specific need and the device is likely to improve movement and function.

Whatever the treatment, do not start, stop or alter prescribed medication without discussing it with an appropriate healthcare professional. Medicines have risks, contraindications and possible interactions, so discuss suitable options with your GP or pharmacist.

## Exercise and strengthening

For most people with knee osteoarthritis, appropriate exercise is an important part of management. It can support muscle strength, joint movement, physical function, balance, confidence and general health. Start with an amount that feels manageable and build gradually rather than chasing a particular target immediately.

One gentle option is seated knee straightening: sit securely on a stable chair, slowly straighten one knee as far as feels comfortable, pause briefly if comfortable, then lower the foot with control. Avoid kicking or forcing the knee straight, and stop if the exercise causes sharp, severe or unusual pain.

Stronger muscles help support the knee during everyday movement. Depending on your ability, strengthening may target the thigh, hip and other muscles involved in walking and standing; a physiotherapist can help you choose exercises that match your current strength and symptoms. Walking, cycling, swimming, water-based exercise and seated exercise can all have a role, and our companion article on knee arthritis exercises goes into the detail.

## Day-to-day self-care

Pacing means balancing activity and rest before symptoms become overwhelming: manageable activity, a short break or easier task, then manageable activity again, rather than a good day spent doing everything followed by a long recovery. Short periods of rest can help when your knee is particularly painful or tired, but prolonged inactivity can contribute to stiffness and reduced strength.

Some people find gentle warmth soothing for stiffness or aching, and a wrapped cold pack soothing when a knee feels painful or swollen. Protect your skin, avoid excessive temperatures, and never put ice directly onto bare skin. A suddenly hot, very swollen knee should not simply be treated as ordinary arthritis stiffness.

## Making stairs and chairs easier

- Stairs: use a handrail, take your time, avoid carrying unnecessarily heavy items, reduce repeated trips, and keep frequently used items on the same floor where practical. If stairs feel unsafe, ask an occupational therapist or physiotherapist for individual advice.
- Chairs: choose a firmer chair, use a slightly higher seat, position your feet securely, use armrests if appropriate, and move towards the front of the chair before standing. If you regularly struggle to stand safely, seek advice rather than relying on unstable furniture.
- Footwear: comfortable, supportive shoes that fit properly, fasten securely and provide reasonable grip can help you feel more secure. There is no single shoe that is best for everyone.
- Walking aids: a walking stick can help some people feel safer, but correct height and technique matter, so ask a physiotherapist whether one is appropriate and how to use it.

## Weight management, handled without blame

For people with knee osteoarthritis who are overweight or living with obesity, NICE recommends discussing weight management as part of treatment, because losing weight can improve quality of life and physical function and reduce pain for some people. Body weight is influenced by many factors, and joint pain itself can make physical activity more difficult, so the approach should be supportive, not blaming.

## Flare days, and when to get checked

During a knee flare, reduce demanding activities, break tasks into smaller parts, take short rests, keep the knee gently moving if comfortable, use heat or cold cautiously, follow your existing treatment plan, and ask for help with difficult tasks. Do not change prescribed medication yourself, and contact your healthcare team if the flare is severe, unusual or not settling.

See a GP if pain is persistent, symptoms repeatedly return, swelling continues, movement is becoming increasingly restricted, pain affects sleep or daily life, your knee repeatedly gives way, or symptoms change significantly. New symptoms should not automatically be attributed to existing arthritis.

> **When it is urgent**
>
> Seek urgent medical advice if a knee becomes suddenly very painful, hot or significantly swollen, particularly if you feel feverish, shivery or generally unwell; a hot, very painful and swollen joint can sometimes indicate infection or another urgent problem. After a significant injury, seek prompt assessment if you cannot put weight through the leg, the knee has changed shape, there is severe swelling, you cannot move the knee normally, or you have numbness or loss of sensation.

## Key takeaways

- Knee arthritis can cause pain, stiffness, swelling and reduced mobility; osteoarthritis is a common cause, but other forms of arthritis can affect the knees too.
- Appropriate exercise and strengthening are an important part of knee osteoarthritis management.
- Pacing, short rests, cautious heat or cold, comfortable footwear and practical adaptations make everyday activities more manageable.
- Weight management may help some people and should be approached without blame.
- Do not change prescribed medication yourself, and get new or suddenly severe symptoms assessed.

## Frequently asked questions

### What does knee osteoarthritis feel like?

Knee osteoarthritis may cause pain and stiffness during or after activity, stiffness after inactivity, reduced movement and occasional swelling. Symptoms can vary considerably between people.

### Should I rest an arthritic knee?

Short periods of rest can help when symptoms are difficult, but prolonged inactivity can contribute to stiffness and loss of strength. Aim for a balance between rest and comfortable movement.

### Does knee arthritis always lead to knee replacement?

No. Many people manage knee arthritis without joint replacement. Surgery is generally considered when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical treatments are no longer providing enough benefit.

### When should I worry about knee arthritis pain?

Seek medical advice for persistent, worsening or unexplained knee symptoms. A suddenly hot, severely painful or significantly swollen knee, particularly with fever or feeling unwell, needs urgent medical assessment.

## A gentle next step

Living with arthritis in the knees does not mean you have to stop moving or give up activities that matter to you. The aim is a sustainable balance between movement, strengthening, pacing, rest and appropriate treatment. A physiotherapist or occupational therapist can provide individual support when needed, and you can explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
